BXL-2425-00008-v22.headline: Let the Region keep running without an approved 2025 budget: unlock month-by-month emergency credits to pay for the administration through January, February and March 2025.
BXL-2425-00008-v22.source_brief:
Six months after the June elections the Region still has no new government and no full 2025 budget, so this text keeps the lights on a different way: it releases "provisional twelfths" — monthly slices of last year's budget — to pay salaries, services and bills for the first quarter of 2025. Vote it through and the administration keeps running; reject it and the Region has no legal basis to spend in January.

- **Budgeting by stopgap.** Instead of a proper 2025 budget debated line by line, the caretaker government asks for permission to spend by reference to the 2024 budget, three months at a time.
- **A watchdog cried foul.** The independent Cour des comptes was given only five working days to review the text and issued an unfavourable opinion, saying the three-twelfths rule was exceeded in places without proper justification.
- **Against a heavy backdrop.** Regional debt was cited in debate as having climbed from 4 billion euros in 2017 to about 14 billion euros now.
- **The rub:** voting yes guarantees public services don't stop — but it also signs off on spending with weak oversight and lets the political deadlock continue without a real budget being put on the table.
deep_facts: The text is the "projet d'ordonnance de finances ouvrant des crédits provisoires pour les mois de janvier, février et mars 2025 sur le budget de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale pour l'année budgétaire 2025" (A-47) (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).

It allows the Region to spend during the first quarter of 2025 by reference to the 2024 initial budget, in the absence of a full 2025 budget; the caretaker government is in affaires courantes following the June 2024 elections, with no new government formed more than six months later (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).

The Cour des comptes (Rekenhof) issued an unfavourable opinion on the text, stating it had only five working days to analyse it, which it deemed insufficient; it noted the three-twelfths rule (règle des trois douzièmes) was exceeded in numerous places and that appropriate justification notes were missing (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).

Debate referenced an attempt to subject the Cour des comptes' audits to a steering committee including representatives of the Brussels finance/budget minister, later withdrawn at the Court's request (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).
Regional debt was cited as having risen from 4 billion euros in 2017 to about 14 billion euros at the time of debate (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).
The Region's A+ rating with stable outlook was referenced, along with a debt-ratio threshold of 210% noted as already exceeded (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).

Amendments tabled would reduce several provisional credits back towards the standard three-twelfths: for the Parliament's credits (programme 100, mission 34) to 3.6 twelfths instead of fourteen; for provisions management (programme 043, mission 36) to three twelfths instead of twelve; for the titres-services scheme (programme 048, mission 44) to four twelfths of the 2024 initial budget; and for the Fonds régional bruxellois de refinancement des trésoreries communales (programme 253, mission 40) from twelve to a little under eleven twelfths (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).

The amendments were stated not to affect public-service operations, public-sector salaries, the employment of domestic-help workers (aides ménagères / huishoudhulpen) or the functioning of approved titres-services firms (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).

The Kanal-Centre Pompidou cultural project was cited in the wider debate at a cost of at least 172 million euros, with 185 million euros referenced as the contractual figure, 180 million engaged and 164 million liquidated to the Fondation Kanal (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).
The project of ordinance, once adopted, is submitted to the government for sanction ("soumis à la sanction du gouvernement") (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).
BXL-2425-00008-v22.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- Provisional twelfths are the legal life-support of a region without a government: they guarantee continuity but freeze policy, since no new spending choices can be made — only last year's pattern, sliced monthly.
- The Cour des comptes' five-day window and unfavourable opinion are the real flashpoint: a 'yes' is partly a vote to spend with oversight the watchdog itself called inadequate, which is why several groups back the credits but distance themselves from the underlying budget management.
- The amendments pulling credits back towards three twelfths read as a discipline move — an attempt to limit how far ahead a caretaker government can pre-commit money before negotiators form a real majority.
- Naming Kanal and the debt trajectory in a routine continuity vote turns the stopgap into a proxy fight over whether Brussels can still afford its flagship projects.
BXL-2425-00008-v22.raw_fr: Projet d'ordonnance de finances ouvrant des crédits provisoires pour les mois de janvier, février et mars 2025 sur le budget de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale pour l'année budgétaire 2025. Faute de gouvernement de plein exercice, la Région doit fonctionner avec des douzièmes provisoires, lesquels assurent la continuité des services. La Cour des comptes, n'ayant disposé que de cinq jours ouvrables, a exprimé une opinion défavorable sur ce texte.

BXL-2425-00008-v25.headline: Release extra budget credits to restart and keep paying the Rénolution home-renovation and energy premiums to Brussels households, after the scheme ran out of money and stopped processing applications in August 2024.
BXL-2425-00008-v25.source_brief:
Brussels pays "Rénolution" premiums to help residents insulate and renovate their homes — but the pot ran dry and on 16 August 2024 the Region stopped processing new applications, leaving thousands of households who had already done the work waiting to be paid. This text frees up additional money so those payments can resume.

- **What it funds.** A budget delegation injecting extra credits, split between Bruxelles Environnement and urban.brussels, to clear the backlog of premium claims for 2024 works.
- **Who it touches.** Roughly 60% of Brussels homes pre-date 1970 and are energy-hungry; the premiums are meant to make renovation affordable for ordinary households, not just wealthy ones who can front the cost.
- **A recurring failure.** Debate noted the budget had run out before year-end in both 2023 and 2024 — the scheme is repeatedly "a victim of its own success".
- **The rub:** few argue against helping residents renovate — the fight is whether this money is actually enough and well-targeted, given the government's own cost estimate was challenged as unrealistic and questions over which households qualify went unanswered.
deep_facts: The text is the "projet d'ordonnance portant mise en vigueur de la délibération budgétaire n° 02 du Gouvernement de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale autorisant l'engagement, la liquidation et le paiement des dépenses, à imputer au budget général des dépenses de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale pour l'année budgétaire 2024 concernant la poursuite des paiements des primes Rénolution" (A-44) (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).

Under this budget delegation, 72 million euros in additional credits are injected, split between Bruxelles Environnement and urban.brussels, described as sufficient to meet the premium applications introduced (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).
Processing of premium applications was suspended on 16 August 2024 for lack of budget, after which households could not continue their renovation works (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).
Debate stated the Rénolution premium budgets had been exhausted before year-end in both 2023 and 2024 ("victimes de leur succès") (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).
A figure of 18 million euros was cited as provided for premiums destined to households ("primes destinées aux ménages") (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).

On the related provisional 2025 credit, the budget was said to be provisioned at 66% of the 2024 budget, corresponding to a liquidation credit of 29.6 million euros for 2025 Rénolution premiums managed by Bruxelles Environnement (mission 041) (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).

The government's cost estimate for the measure was cited at 29 million euros, contrasted in debate with 140 million euros spent in the first half of 2024, a comparison one member called unrealistic (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).

Debate flagged an unresolved ambiguity over eligibility — whether the claimant's invoice had to be merely emitted, or also paid, by 31 December 2024 — with a stated risk of back-dated invoices (factures antidatées) (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).

It was noted that close to 60% of Brussels housing dates from before 1970 and is often old and energy-inefficient; concern was raised that renovation can push up rents and that mainly wealthier households benefit from the current premium system (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).

The application portal was said to remain open in 2025, with a call for clear communication to citizens on eligibility conditions; the ordinance, once adopted, is submitted to the government for sanction (CRI, 19 Dec 2024).
BXL-2425-00008-v25.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- The vote is less about whether to help renovators than about cleaning up a budgeting failure: the scheme was stopped mid-year because demand was under-budgeted, and this text retro-funds the gap.
- The unresolved "emitted vs paid by 31 December" question is the real lever — it silently decides which households actually get paid and how big the bill is, which is why members pressed for clarity and warned of back-dated invoices.
- The 29-million-euro estimate set against 140 million euros spent in H1 2024 suggests the credit may again be under-sized, setting up a repeat of the mid-year freeze.
- The structural critique — that premiums favour households able to front the cost, and that renovation can raise rents — frames a citizen's choice between keeping a flawed-but-real subsidy flowing and demanding the scheme be redesigned before more money goes in.
BXL-2425-00008-v25.raw_fr: Projet d'ordonnance portant mise en vigueur de la délibération budgétaire n° 02 concernant la poursuite des paiements des primes Rénolution. Les primes ont été victimes de leur succès et le traitement des demandes a été suspendu le 16 août 2024, faute de budget ; 72 millions d'euros supplémentaires sont injectés, répartis entre Bruxelles Environnement et urban.brussels, pour répondre aux demandes introduites.
